I bet no one was more surprised than the constructor that this appeared on a Tuesday.  The trick is not a Tuesday-level trick.  (How often does a Tuesday even have a trick?)  The clues are not Tuesday-level clues.  Once you've figured out the trick --  I figured it out at GENDER REVEAL -- the puzzle isn't all that hard.  But boy do I feel sorry for the person who only solves on Monday and Tuesday and then had to wrestle this to the ground with no previous experience of such a thing as blank clues.

I had a wonderful time, of course.  It's like having an extra latish-week puzzle in the week.  An interesting grid, nice cluing, and more than a little thinking required from me.  More challenge than I expect on a Tuesday and a lot of fun to solve.

I don't accept “--” as a crossword clue.

It means different things in different puzzles. I know it's a convention: the dash tells us that the answer is clued somewhere else. But that's an unnecessarily vague way to communicate* something that could easily be made explicit.

There's nothing difficult about splitting GENDER REVEAL into two entries and cluing each separately, even with the tedious “With 21-Across…”

My objection is logical: “--” doesn't actually tell us anything. We're simply expected to pretend it does, and that everyone knows what it means.

*A thought I had earlier, in private, that you have to guess.

The word/name Horae (in Greek, Ὧραι) is sometimes rendered in English as "the Hours." Why the confusion? Because the Greek, and Latin, "hora"--the source of the (Norman English) word "hour"--can mean any season or period of time, large or small. "Hora" stems from the Indo-European root "*yóh₁r̥"--make sure you enunciate that subscript "1" clearly!--which is also the source of the (Germanic) word year. Turn, turn, turn. The Horae were generally depicted as a trio, but their names varied depending on which sources you consult--sometimes Eunomia, Dike, and Eirene; sometimes Thallo, Auxo, and Carpo; and sometimes Nicole, Julianne, and Meryl. Among other tasks, one of the Horae's duties was to act as fluffers for the goddess Aphrodite. Why, here comes one now!: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hgO3JugGMm0&list=RDhgO3JugGMm0&start_radio=1 (One of my all-time favorite bits of orchestral writing.)
